claim: Pcdh20 is preferentially expressed in layer 4 (L4) of the neocortex on postnatal day 7 (P7).
source: we found that Pcdh20 is preferentially expressed in L4 on P7 (Figure 1A–A").
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A-A" and described in the text.

claim: Pcdh20 is expressed beneath the marginal zone (MZ) in the somatosensory cortex on E18.5.
source: On E18.5, Pcdh20 was expressed beneath the MZ (Figure 1B,B') in the somatosensory cortex, where a large fraction of the "future L4 neurons" resides after radial neuronal migration (Ajioka and Nakajima, 2005)
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B,B' and cited reference.

claim: Pcdh20 expression is weak in the E14.0 and E16.5 neocortex.
source: We only found weak expression of Pcdh20 in the E14.0 and E16.5 neocortex (Figure 1C,C',D,D'), where "future L4 neurons" were being produced and were migrating (Ajioka and Nakajima, 2005).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C,C',D,D' and cited reference.

claim: Pcdh20 mRNA expression levels in early developmental stages are much lower than those in postnatal stages.
source: The expression levels of Pcdh20 were also analyzed by quantitative RT-PCR, and it was confirmed that the expression levels of Pcdh20 mRNA in the early stages were much lower than those in the postnatal stages (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Pcdh20 begins to be expressed strongly only at a relatively late stage of radial migration toward the MZ.
source: These results suggest that Pcdh20 begins to be expressed strongly only at a relatively late stage of radial migration toward the MZ.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal expression pattern data shown in Figure 1.

claim: PC20sh markedly reduces the protein expression level of Pcdh20 compared to control shRNA (CONsh).
source: We found that expression of an shRNA vector targeting Pcdh20 (hereinafter referred to as PC20sh) was associated with a markedly reduced protein expression level of Pcdh20 as compared with that of a control shRNA (CONsh) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: PC20sh_mut does not significantly affect the expression level of Pcdh20.
source: On the other hand, expression of a mutant shRNA vector harboring three point mutations in PC20sh (PC20sh_mut) did not significantly affect the expression level of Pcdh20 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: PC20sh markedly decreases the endogenous expression levels of Pcdh20 mRNA in primary cortical cultures.
source: Furthermore, this knockdown vector was found to markedly decrease the endogenous expression levels of Pcdh20 mRNA (Figure 2B) as well as protein (Figure 2C) in primary cortical cultures.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2B and immunoblotting data in Figure 2C.

claim: Most GFP-positive cells with CONsh or PC20sh_mut in the somatosensory cortex are located in L4 at P7.
source: In the controls, most of the GFP-positive cells with CONsh or PC20sh_mut in the somatosensory cortex were located in L4 (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by in vivo electroporation data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Electroporation of PC20sh changes the laminar location of GFP-positive cells to more superficial layers.
source: On the other hand, electroporation of PC20sh changed the laminar location of the GFP-positive cells to more superficial layers (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by in vivo electroporation data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: An shRNA vector targeting the 3'UTR of the Pcdh20 gene disrupts the laminar positioning of electroporated cells.
source: In addition, another shRNA vector targeting the 3'UTR of the Pcdh20 gene also disrupted the laminar positioning of the electroporated cells (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by in vivo electroporation data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Co-introduction of an RNAi-resistant Pcdh20-expressing vector (resPcdh20) with PC20sh recovers the defect of neuronal positioning of PC20sh-expressing cells.
source: The specificity of PC20sh for Pcdh20 was further confirmed by an experiment in which co-introduction of an RNAi-resistant Pcdh20-expressing vector (resPcdh20) with PC20sh recovered the defect of neuronal positioning of the PC20sh-expressing cells (Figure 2F,G; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2F,G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pcdh20 knockdown in deeper layer neurons (L5 and L6) hardly affects cell positioning.
source: We also analyzed the effects of Pcdh20 knockdown on deep layer neurons by transfecting the shRNA vectors on E12.5, when L5 and L6 neurons were expected to be produced. We found that Pcdh20 knockdown in the deeper layer neurons hardly affected the cell positioning (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C), suggesting the specific function of Pcdh20 in L4 neurons.
evidence: Supported by in vivo electroporation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Pcdh20 is required for correct positioning of the cells in L4.
source: These results together suggest the requirement of Pcdh20 for correct positioning of the cells in L4.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing malpositioning upon Pcdh20 knockdown and rescue by resPcdh20.

claim: The function of Pcdh20 is cell-autonomous.
source: This function of Pcdh20 appeared to be cell-autonomous, since sequential electroporation of mCherry fluorescent protein, followed by a mixture of GFP and PC20sh, showed that the Pcdh20 knockdown did not change the positioning of the mCherry-single positive control cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by sequential electroporation experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Ectopic expression of Pcdh20 does not cause repositioning of L2/3 neurons to L4.
source: The results revealed that ectopic expression of Pcdh20 did not cause repositioning of L2/3 neurons to L4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F)
evidence: Supported by ectopic expression experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Ectopic expression of Pcdh20 causes L2/3 neurons to be located more broadly in L2/3 compared to control cells.
source: but caused the same cells to be located more broadly in L2/3 as compared with the control cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F)
evidence: Supported by ectopic expression experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Pcdh20 expression by itself is not sufficient to change the location and morphology of L2/3 neurons to L4.
source: suggesting that Pcdh20 expression by itself is not sufficient to change the location and morphology of L2/3 neurons to L4, and that some other factor(s) are also involved in the Pcdh20-dependent positioning of the L4 neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the ectopic expression experiment results.

claim: On E16.5 and E18.0, few differences are observed between control and Pcdh20-knockdown brains in neuronal positioning.
source: On E16.5 and E18.0, few differences were observed between the control and Pcdh20-knockdown brains (Figure 2H,I,L and data not shown).
evidence: Supported by time-course experiment data shown in Figure 2H,I,L.

claim: At P2, Pcdh20-knockdown cells are located in a slightly more superficial position than control cells.
source: In contrast, analysis of the P2 brains, in which the "future L4 neurons" had started to form a layer structure beneath the primitive L2/3, revealed that the Pcdh20-knockdown cells were located in a slightly more superficial position than that in the controls (Figure 2J,K,M).
evidence: Supported by time-course experiment data shown in Figure 2J,K,M.

claim: Pcdh20 plays an important role in the post-migratory stage when neurons are beneath the MZ and start to express Pcdh20 strongly.
source: These data suggest that Pcdh20 may play an important role in the post-migratory stage, when the neurons are already present beneath the MZ and start to express Pcdh20 strongly.
evidence: Inferred from time-course experiments showing effects only after migration is complete.

claim: Most GFP-positive cells in control samples express Rorb at P7.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis of the P7 brains showed that while most of the GFP-positive cells in the control samples expressed Rorb, the percentage of Rorb-positive cells among the GFP-positive cells was markedly decreased by knockdown of Pcdh20 (Figure 3A–C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The percentage of Rorb-positive cells among GFP-positive cells is markedly decreased by Pcdh20 knockdown at P7.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis of the P7 brains showed that while most of the GFP-positive cells in the control samples expressed Rorb, the percentage of Rorb-positive cells among the GFP-positive cells was markedly decreased by knockdown of Pcdh20 (Figure 3A–C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Expression of KCNH5 is not observed in ectopically located GFP-positive cells by Pcdh20 knockdown.
source: Expression of KCNH5 (a potassium voltage-gated channel, subfamily H), another marker of L4 neurons, was also not observed in the ectopically located GFP-positive cells by Pcdh20 knockdown (Figure 3D,E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3D,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Malpositioned neurons by Pcdh20 knockdown do not grossly change the growth of thalamocortical axons (TCAs).
source: Moreover, immunostaining for NetrinG1, a marker of thalamocortical axons (TCAs), showed that the malpositioned neurons by Pcdh20 knockdown did not grossly change the growth of TCAs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K,L).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1K,L.

claim: Malpositioned Pcdh20-knockdown neurons lost the characteristics of L4 neurons.
source: These results suggest that the malpositioned Pcdh20-knockdown neurons lost the characteristics of L4 neurons.
evidence: Inferred from loss of L4 markers (Rorb, KCNH5) in Pcdh20-knockdown cells.

claim: Pcdh20 knockdown is associated with a markedly increased percentage of Lhx2-expressing cells.
source: On the other hand, while the expression of Lhx2, a L2/3 marker (Nakagawa et al., 1999), was detected in only a small fraction of the GFP-positive neurons in the controls, Pcdh20 knockdown was associated with a markedly increased percentage of Lhx2-expressing cells (Figure 3F–H; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3F–H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F, with citation.

claim: Pcdh20 knockdown is associated with an increase in the percentage of neurons positive for Satb2.
source: We also found that Pcdh20 knockdown was associated with an increase in the percentage of neurons positive for Satb2, a callosal neuron maker (Alcamo et al., 2008; Britanova et al., 2008) (Figure 3I–K; Figure 3—figure supplement 1G,H)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3I–K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G,H, with citations.

claim: Pcdh20 knockdown is associated with an increase in the percentage of neurons positive for Tbr1.
source: and Tbr1, a L2/3 and L6 marker (Hevner et al., 2001) (Figure 3L–N; Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3L–N and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J, with citation.

claim: Pcdh20 knockdown causes neurons destined for L4 to acquire L2/3 characteristics at a molecular marker level.
source: These results suggest that Pcdh20 knockdown caused the neurons destined for L4 to acquire L2/3 characteristics, at least at a molecular marker level.
evidence: Inferred from increased expression of L2/3 markers (Lhx2, Satb2, Tbr1) in Pcdh20-knockdown cells.

claim: On E18.0, Rorb expression is almost exclusively detected in L5, and Lhx2 expression is uniform in all superficial layer neurons.
source: However, since Rorb expression was almost exclusively detected in L5, and Lhx2 expression was uniform in all the superficial layer neurons (both future L2/3 and L4) on E18.0 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1M–P), we could not assess the specification/differentiation of L2/3 and L4 at this stage.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1M–P.

claim: On P2, Rorb expression is detected in control L4 neurons but not in Pcdh20-knockdown cells.
source: On P2, Rorb expression was detected in control L4 neurons, but not in Pcdh20-knockdown cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q,R), similar to the finding in the P7 neocortex
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q,R.

claim: At P2, Lhx2 expression is still relatively uniform in all superficial layer neurons.
source: although Lhx2 expression was still relatively uniform in all superficial layer neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1S,T)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1S,T.

claim: At least some laminar characteristics begin to be regulated by Pcdh20 by P2.
source: suggesting that at least some of the laminar characteristics had begun to be regulated by Pcdh20 by this stage.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Rorb expression differences are evident at P2.

claim: Many L4 neurons labeled by electroporation on E14.0 extend axons locally within the ipsilateral cortex.
source: Normally, many L4 neurons, which can be labeled by electroporation on E14.0, extend axons locally within the ipsilateral cortex, while most of the L2/3 neurons, which can be labeled by electroporation on E15.0, extend axons to the contralateral cortex (Molyneaux et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to established knowledge.

claim: Most L2/3 neurons labeled by electroporation on E15.0 extend axons to the contralateral cortex.
source: Normally, many L4 neurons, which can be labeled by electroporation on E14.0, extend axons locally within the ipsilateral cortex, while most of the L2/3 neurons, which can be labeled by electroporation on E15.0, extend axons to the contralateral cortex (Molyneaux et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to established knowledge.

claim: The percentage of retrogradely labeled neurons in L2/3 is much higher than that in L4.
source: We first confirmed that the percentage of retrogradely labeled neurons in L2/3 was much higher than that in L4 (Figure 4A,C,D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 4A,C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: Pcdh20 knockdown is associated with a substantial increase in the percentage of retrogradely labeled neurons in electroporated cells.
source: Interestingly, Pcdh20 knockdown was associated with a substantial increase in the percentage of the retrogradely labeled neurons in the electroporated cells (Figure 4B,D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that these axons projected to the contralateral cortex.
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 4B,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Neurons labeled on E14.0 require Pcdh20 for proper L4 specification and acquire L2/3 characteristics in the face of Pcdh20 knockdown.
source: These results suggest that the neurons labeled on E14.0, which normally populate L4, require Pcdh20 for proper L4 specification, and instead acquire L2/3 characteristics in the face of Pcdh20 knockdown.
evidence: Inferred from axonal projection pattern changes and molecular marker changes upon Pcdh20 knockdown.

claim: Almost all control L4 neurons show the morphology of stellate neurons, which extend their dendrites radially in many directions.
source: Histochemical visualization with biocytin loaded through the recording patch pipette revealed that almost all control L4 neurons showed the morphology of stellate neurons, which extend their dendrites radially in many directions (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by biocytin labeling data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Malpositioned Pcdh20-knockdown neurons possess a thick apical dendrite with terminal arborization in L1 and a thin axon extending toward the ventricular side.
source: On the other hand, the malpositioned Pcdh20-knockdown neurons possessed a thick apical dendrite with terminal arborization in the L1 and a thin axon extending toward the ventricular side (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), similar to the control pyramidal neurons in L2/3 (Figure 4G; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by biocytin labeling data shown in Figure 4F,G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: Pcdh20-knockdown cells differ in some characteristics from control L4 cells while being similar in some characteristics to L2/3 cells.
source: We also found that the Pcdh20-knockdown cells differed in some, if not in all, characteristics from the control L4 cells, while being similar in some characteristics to the L2/3 cells (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Characteristics that confer resemblance of Pcdh20-knockdown cells to L2/3 neurons include the frequency of sEPSCs, half width of the action potential, and the input resistance.
source: These characteristics that conferred resemblance to the L2/3 neurons included the frequency of sEPSCs, half width of the action potential, and the input resistance (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The electrophysiological properties of malpositioned cells by Pcdh20 knockdown resemble those of surrounding control L2/3 cells.
source: These data suggest that the electrophysiological properties of the malpositioned cells by Pcdh20 knockdown came to resemble those of the surrounding control L2/3 cells.
evidence: Inferred from electrophysiological measurements showing similarity to L2/3 cells.

claim: Knockdown of Pcdh20 causes neurons destined for L4 to acquire L2/3 neuronal characteristics including morphology, electrophysiology, molecular markers, and axonal projections.
source: These changes in the electrophysiological properties and cell morphology, together with those in the expressions of molecular markers, strongly suggest that knockdown of Pcdh20 expression cause the neurons destined for L4 to acquire L2/3 neuronal characteristics.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including morphology, electrophysiology, and molecular markers.

claim: The conversion of L4 to L2/3 characteristics by Pcdh20 knockdown is incomplete.
source: However, this conversion was incomplete, because the membrane capacitance of the Pcdh20-knockdown cells was almost the same as that of the control L4 cells and less than a half of that of the control L2/3 cells (Figure 4H); thus, the Pcdh20-knockdown cells still remained small in size, like the L4 neurons.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data showing membrane capacitance differences in Figure 4H.

claim: Pcdh20-knockdown neurons tend to possess less well-developed basal dendrites compared to control L2/3 neurons.
source: We also noticed that Pcdh20-knockdown neurons tended to possess less well-developed basal dendrites as compared to the control L2/3 neurons (Figure 4F,G; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by morphological observations in Figure 4F,G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The percentage of Rorb-positive cells in the GFP+/BrdU– population is markedly decreased by Pcdh20 knockdown.
source: Triple immunostaining of P7 brain sections for GFP, BrdU and Rorb revealed that the percentage of Rorb-positive cells in the GFP+/BrdU– population was markedly decreased by knockdown of Pcdh20 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C), suggesting that Pcdh20 knockdown perturbed L4 specification of the postmitotic cells.
evidence: Supported by BrdU labeling and immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: Pcdh20 knockdown perturbs L4 specification of postmitotic cells.
source: Triple immunostaining of P7 brain sections for GFP, BrdU and Rorb revealed that the percentage of Rorb-positive cells in the GFP+/BrdU– population was markedly decreased by knockdown of Pcdh20 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C), suggesting that Pcdh20 knockdown perturbed L4 specification of the postmitotic cells.
evidence: Inferred from decreased Rorb expression in postmitotic (GFP+/BrdU–) cells upon Pcdh20 knockdown.

claim: The effect of Pcdh20 knockdown is not influenced by whether the knockdown vector is introduced into a postmitotic population or a mitotic population.
source: The extent of decrease in the percentage of Rorb-positive cells was comparable in all cell populations (Figure 3C), suggesting that the effect of Pcdh20 knockdown was not influenced by whether the knockdown vector was introduced into a postmitotic population or a mitotic population.
evidence: Inferred from comparable effects across different cell populations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Pcdh20 knockdown does not alter cell cycle progression in the VZ/SVZ cells.
source: Importantly, the proportions of BrdU-negative cells in the entire population of GFP-positive cells were almost the same between the control and knockdown cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that Pcdh20 knockdown did not alter cell cycle progression in the VZ/SVZ cells.
evidence: Supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: A Tα1-driven resPcdh20 expression vector rescues the phenotype of malpositioning caused by Pcdh20 knockdown.
source: We found that a Tα1-driven resPcdh20 expression vector rescued the phenotype of malpositioning of the cells caused by Pcdh20 knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E,F), further suggesting the important function of Pcdh20 in postmitotic neurons.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E,F.

claim: Postmitotic expression of Pcdh20 is essential for its functions.
source: We further investigated whether the postmitotic expression of Pcdh20 may be essential for its functions, by conducting a rescue experiment using a neuron-specific Tα1 (α1-tubulin) promoter-driven expression vector to express resPcdh20 (Gloster et al., 1994). We found that a Tα1-driven resPcdh20 expression vector rescued the phenotype of malpositioning of the cells caused by Pcdh20 knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E,F), further suggesting the important function of Pcdh20 in postmitotic neurons.
evidence: Inferred from rescue experiment using neuron-specific promoter, with citation.

claim: DN-RhoA-electroporated neurons are located more superficially compared with control neurons.
source: The DN-RhoA-electroporated neurons were located more superficially as compared with the control neurons (Figure 5A,B), similar to the effect of Pcdh20 knockdown
evidence: Supported by in vivo electroporation data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: RhoA signaling is required for correct cell positioning of L4 neurons.
source: We first examined whether RhoA signaling was required for correct cell positioning of the L4 neurons. We inhibited RhoA signaling in the future L4 neurons by introducing a dominant-negative form of RhoA (T19N, DN-RhoA). The DN-RhoA-electroporated neurons were located more superficially as compared with the control neurons (Figure 5A,B), similar to the effect of Pcdh20 knockdown, suggesting that these two genes may function in the same signaling pathway to ensure correct positioning of L4 neurons.
evidence: Inferred from DN-RhoA causing similar malpositioning as Pcdh20 knockdown.

claim: Pcdh20 and RhoA may function in the same signaling pathway to ensure correct positioning of L4 neurons.
source: suggesting that these two genes may function in the same signaling pathway to ensure correct positioning of L4 neurons.
evidence: Inferred from similar phenotypes of Pcdh20 knockdown and DN-RhoA expression.

claim: There is no significant difference in cell positioning between control and DN-RhoA expressing cells at E18.0.
source: We found that there was no significant difference in cell positioning between control and DN-RhoA expressing cells at least at the concentration/condition we used (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the DN-RhoA-expressing neurons settle in the ridge of the CP similarly to normal cells after radial migration
evidence: Supported by time-course experiment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The phenotype of DN-RhoA at P7 is caused mainly by events after radial migration toward the brain surface is completed.
source: Therefore, the phenotype observed at P7 (Figure 5A) was thought to be caused mainly by the event after radial migration toward the brain surface is completed.
evidence: Inferred from no difference at E18.0 but differences at P7.

claim: Co-expression of CA-RhoA with PC20sh rescues the malpositioning of future L4 neurons caused by Pcdh20 knockdown.
source: The results revealed that co-expression of CA-RhoA with PC20sh indeed rescued the malpositioning of future L4 neurons caused by Pcdh20 knockdown (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The loss of Rorb expression by Pcdh20 knockdown is restored by co-expression of CA-RhoA with PC20sh.
source: Moreover, we examined the misspecification phenotype associated with Pcdh20 knockdown and found that the loss of Rorb expression by Pcdh20 knockdown was also restored by co-expression of CA-RhoA with PC20sh (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5E–H.

claim: RhoA functions downstream of Pcdh20.
source: These results suggest that RhoA functions downstream of Pcdh20.
evidence: Inferred from CA-RhoA rescuing Pcdh20 knockdown phenotypes.

claim: The proportions of Rorb- and KCNH5-positive cells among GFP-positive cells located in L2–4 are dramatically decreased by Dcx knockdown.
source: The proportions of Rorb- as well as KCNH5-positive cells among the GFP-positive cells located in L2–4 were dramatically decreased by Dcx knockdown (Figure 6A–E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by Dcx knockdown experiment data shown in Figure 6A–E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: The proportions of Lhx2- and Satb2-positive cells are markedly increased by Dcx knockdown.
source: Correspondingly, the proportions of Lhx2- as well as Satb2-positive cells were markedly increased by Dcx knockdown (Figure 6F–K; Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–H), implying the importance of cell positioning.
evidence: Supported by Dcx knockdown experiment data shown in Figure 6F–K and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: No change in the proportion of Tbr1-positive cells is noted in association with Dcx knockdown.
source: On the other hand, no change in the proportion of Tbr1-positive cells was noted in association with Dcx knockdown (Figure 6L–N; Figure 6—figure supplement 1I,J), suggesting that Tbr1 expression may not be regulated simply by cell positioning.
evidence: Supported by Dcx knockdown experiment data shown in Figure 6L–N and Figure 6—figure supplement 1I,J.

claim: Tbr1 expression may not be regulated simply by cell positioning.
source: On the other hand, no change in the proportion of Tbr1-positive cells was noted in association with Dcx knockdown (Figure 6L–N; Figure 6—figure supplement 1I,J), suggesting that Tbr1 expression may not be regulated simply by cell positioning.
evidence: Inferred from Tbr1 expression not changing with Dcx knockdown-induced malpositioning.

claim: The majority (72%) of Dcx-knockdown neurons positioned in L4 express Rorb, whereas none of the neurons in L2/3 express this marker.
source: The majority of the neurons positioned in L4 expressed Rorb (72%), whereas none of the neurons in L2/3 expressed this marker (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of Rorb expression in Dcx-knockdown neurons shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The ultimate cell positioning determines most of the neuronal characteristics of neurons labeled on E14.0, that is, into L2/3 or L4 neurons.
source: These results suggest that the ultimate cell positioning determines most of the neuronal characteristics of the neurons labeled on E14.0, that is, into L2/3 or L4 neurons.
evidence: Inferred from Dcx knockdown experiments showing position-dependent marker expression.

claim: Neurons accidentally positioned in L4 in the absence of Pcdh20 (with Dcx knockdown) express Rorb.
source: We found that the neurons were indeed positioned in a random manner throughout the neocortex (Figure 6—figure supplement 1N–P), and that many of the neurons that were accidentally positioned in L4 expressed Rorb even in the absence of Pcdh20 (Figure 6O–Q), suggesting that Pcdh20 controls L4 specification indirectly.
evidence: Supported by double knockdown experiment data shown in Figure 6O–Q and Figure 6—figure supplement 1N–P.

claim: Pcdh20 controls L4 specification indirectly.
source: suggesting that Pcdh20 controls L4 specification indirectly.
evidence: Inferred from rescue of L4 characteristics by repositioning to L4 even without Pcdh20.

claim: Pcdh20 knockdown does not change the percentage of Rorb-positive cells in in vitro primary cortical culture.
source: We found that Pcdh20 knockdown did not change the percentage of Rorb-positive cells (Figure 6R), suggesting that Pcdh20 requires the in vivo cell environment to exert its function on the L4 specification.
evidence: Supported by in vitro culture experiment data shown in Figure 6R.

claim: Pcdh20 requires the in vivo cell environment to exert its function on L4 specification.
source: We found that Pcdh20 knockdown did not change the percentage of Rorb-positive cells (Figure 6R), suggesting that Pcdh20 requires the in vivo cell environment to exert its function on the L4 specification.
evidence: Inferred from Pcdh20 knockdown having no effect in vitro but having effects in vivo.

claim: Pcdh20 specifies L4 identity through controlling the cell positioning of future L4 neurons.
source: These results altogether strongly suggest that Pcdh20 specifies L4 identity through controlling the cell positioning of future L4 neurons.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including rescue by repositioning and lack of effect in vitro.

claim: Pcdh20-knockdown neurons possess a higher number of neurites than control neurons in in vitro culture.
source: In addition, in a similar culture condition, Pcdh20-knockdown neurons were found to possess a higher number of neurites than the control neurons (Figure 6S–U), suggesting that Pcdh20 might, at least to some extent, directly regulate the neuronal morphology.
evidence: Supported by in vitro culture morphology data shown in Figure 6S–U.

claim: Pcdh20 might, at least to some extent, directly regulate neuronal morphology.
source: In addition, in a similar culture condition, Pcdh20-knockdown neurons were found to possess a higher number of neurites than the control neurons (Figure 6S–U), suggesting that Pcdh20 might, at least to some extent, directly regulate the neuronal morphology.
evidence: Inferred from increased neurite number in Pcdh20-knockdown neurons in vitro.

claim: The timing of invasion of thalamocortical axons (TCAs) into the neocortex and immature L4 (perinatal stages) is well correlated with that of maturation of L4 neurons.
source: We focused on TCAs, because the timing of invasion of these axons into the neocortex and the immature L4 (perinatal stages) is well correlated with that of maturation of the L4 neurons (Lopez-Bendito and Molnar, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to established knowledge.

claim: TCAs invading upward from the deeper part of the CP may provide a positional cue to cortical neurons.
source: It is thus possible that TCAs invading upward from the deeper part of the CP may provide a positional cue to the cortical neurons.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on timing correlation.

claim: TCAs are markedly decreased in the brains of Pcdh10 (OL-pc) knockout mice.
source: Immunohistochemistry for NetrinG1, a TCA-specific marker, revealed a marked decrease of the TCAs in the brains of the Pcdh10 (OL-pc) knockout mice (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Expression of Rorb is markedly decreased in Pcdh10 (OL-pc) knockout mice.
source: We found that expression of Rorb was markedly decreased in Pcdh10 (OL-pc) knockout mice (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7C–E.

claim: Expressions of Lhx2 and Tbr1 are increased in the Pcdh10 (OL-pc) knockout neocortex.
source: In parallel with the decrease in the expression of the L4 marker, expressions of Lhx2 and Tbr1, both of which are not expressed in L4 in the control neocortex, were increased in the mutant neocortex (Figure 7F–K).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7F–K.

claim: Neurons destined to become L4 neurons lose their L4 identity and acquire some L2/3 characteristics in the absence of TCAs.
source: These results suggest that the neurons that are destined to become L4 neurons lose their L4 identity and instead acquire some of the L2/3 characteristics, presumably because of the absence of the TCAs.
evidence: Inferred from marker expression changes in Pcdh10 (OL-pc) knockout mice lacking TCAs.

claim: TCAs might provide a positional cue to immature L4 neurons.
source: Moreover, these results are similar to the misspecification phenotype of the malpositioned neurons by Pcdh20 or Dcx knockdown, suggesting that TCAs might provide a positional cue to immature L4 neurons.
evidence: Inferred from similarity of phenotypes between TCA-deficient mice and Pcdh20/Dcx knockdown.

claim: The laminar identities of neurons within the superficial layers (L2–4) of the CP are not completely specified until the neurons arrive beneath the MZ.
source: We propose that the laminar identities of neurons within the superficial layers (L2–4) of the CP are not completely specified until the neurons arrive beneath the MZ; the ultimate fates of the L2/3 and L4 neurons are specified in the post-migratory phase according to the positioning of the cells.
evidence: Inferred from all experimental results showing position-dependent specification.

claim: The ultimate fates of L2/3 and L4 neurons are specified in the post-migratory phase according to the positioning of the cells.
source: We propose that the laminar identities of neurons within the superficial layers (L2–4) of the CP are not completely specified until the neurons arrive beneath the MZ; the ultimate fates of the L2/3 and L4 neurons are specified in the post-migratory phase according to the positioning of the cells.
evidence: Inferred from all experimental results showing position-dependent specification.

claim: Future L4 neurons are positioned in the deeper part of the superficial layers in a Pcdh20-RhoA-dependent manner after radial migration to the top of the CP.
source: In this model, "future L4 neurons" are positioned in the deeper part of the superficial layers in a Pcdh20-RhoA-dependent manner after radial migration to the top of the CP, and then differentiate into mature L4 neurons, presumably by receiving signals from TCAs (Figure 7L).
evidence: Inferred from experimental results and presented as a model in Figure 7L.

claim: Future L4 neurons differentiate into mature L4 neurons, presumably by receiving signals from TCAs.
source: In this model, "future L4 neurons" are positioned in the deeper part of the superficial layers in a Pcdh20-RhoA-dependent manner after radial migration to the top of the CP, and then differentiate into mature L4 neurons, presumably by receiving signals from TCAs (Figure 7L).
evidence: Inferred from TCA-deficient mouse phenotypes and presented as a model.

claim: The processes that take place after radial migration are precisely regulated and critical for correct laminar positioning of at least the future L4 neurons.
source: Although post-migratory neurons were generally thought to just pile up on the earlier-settled neurons after radial migration, our results imply that the processes that take place after radial migration are also precisely regulated and are critical for correct laminar positioning of at least the "future L4 neurons".
evidence: Inferred from all experimental results showing post-migratory regulation.

claim: The Relnrl/Relnrl neocortex contains an almost normal set of neuronal subtypes despite inverted and disorganized cortical laminar structure.
source: In previous studies, the Relnrl/Relnrlneocortex, in which the cortical laminar structure is largely inverted and considerably disorganized, was shown to contain an almost normal set of neuronal subtypes (Dehay and Kennedy, 2007; Hevner et al., 2003; Polleux et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: When future L2/3 neurons are induced to localize in L5, they do not acquire the characteristics of L5 neurons.
source: Another relevant observation is that when future L2/3 neurons were induced to localize in L5, they did not acquire the characteristics of L5 neurons (Ramos et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: A substantial amount of TCAs grow into the Relnrl/Relnrl mutant CP, although they pass a bizarre course.
source: In this mutant, a substantial amount of TCAs was reported to grow into the mutant CP, although they pass a bizarre course (Caviness and Frost, 1983), which could be enough to induce L4 specification.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: L4 specification may occur in postmitotic neurons.
source: Although it has long been supposed that cell fate decision of cortical neurons takes place mainly in the progenitor cells (Dehay and Kennedy, 2007; Molyneaux et al., 2007), our data now suggest that L4 specification may also occur in postmitotic neurons
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including postmitotic Pcdh20 expression and function.

claim: The distribution of Pcdh20-knockdown neurons remains normal before and during radial neuronal migration but becomes disrupted after neurons settle beneath the MZ.
source: Consistent with this finding, the distribution of the Pcdh20-knockdown neurons remained normal before and during radial neuronal migration, but became disrupted after the neurons settled beneath the MZ.
evidence: Supported by time-course experimental data.

claim: Introduction of the Pcdh20-knockdown vector even in a postmitotic population causes misspecification of L4 neurons.
source: Moreover, introduction of the Pcdh20-knockdown vector even in a postmitotic population caused misspecification of the L4 neurons.
evidence: Supported by BrdU labeling experiment data.

claim: Expression of Pcdh20 in postmitotic neurons is able to rescue the phenotypes induced by Pcdh20 knockdown.
source: Finally, expression of Pcdh20 in the postmitotic neurons was able to rescue the phenotypes induced by Pcdh20 knockdown.
evidence: Supported by Tα1 promoter rescue experiment data.

claim: Many subtype-specific genes play roles in postmitotic neurons.
source: This idea, of postmitotic regulation of subtype specification, is also supported by the fact that many subtype-specific genes play roles in postmitotic neurons (Alcamo et al., 2008; Arlotta et al., 2005; Britanova et al., 2008; Kwan et al., 2008; Lai et al., 2008; Leone et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is a high level of plasticity in the identity of postmitotic cortical neurons.
source: and that there is a high level of plasticity in the identity of postmitotic cortical neurons (De la Rossa et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Future L4 neurons have the capacity to differentiate into L2/3 neurons even in the postmitotic stage.
source: These observations suggest that "future L4 neurons" have the capacity to differentiate into L2/3 neurons even in the postmitotic stage.
evidence: Inferred from Pcdh20-knockdown neurons acquiring L2/3 characteristics.

claim: Laminar fates are regulated, at least in part, in the progenitor cells.
source: Our results, however, also suggest regulation, at least in part, of the laminar fates in the progenitor cells, because the Pcdh20-knockdown "future L4 neurons" had "imperfect" characteristics as compared to the normal L2/3 neurons, such as poorly developed basal dendrites and relatively mild conversion of the axonal projection patterns in the knockdown neurons located in L2/3.
evidence: Inferred from incomplete conversion of L4 to L2/3 characteristics.

claim: The effect of dominant-negative RhoA mimics the failure in neuronal positioning induced by Pcdh20 knockdown.
source: We observed that the effect of dominant-negative RhoA mimicked the failure in neuronal positioning induced by Pcdh20 knockdown
evidence: Supported by DN-RhoA experiment data.

claim: CA-RhoA is able to restore the phenotypes of Pcdh20-knockdown neurons.
source: and that CA-RhoA was able to restore the phenotypes of the Pcdh20-knockdown neurons.
evidence: Supported by CA-RhoA rescue experiment data.

claim: The relationship between protocadherin and RhoA has been shown in other systems.
source: The relationship between protocadherin and RhoA has also been shown in other systems (Chung et al., 2007; Unterseher et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss of Pcdh20 primarily leads to dysregulation of dendritic morphogenesis, followed by malpositioning of L4 neurons.
source: We assume that the loss of Pcdh20 primarily leads to dysregulation of dendritic morphogenesis, followed by malpositioning of the L4 neurons
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including in vitro morphology changes.

claim: Pcdh20 knockdown in an in vitro culture results in increased dendritogenesis without altering L4 fate specification.
source: First, Pcdh20 knockdown in an in vitro culture, where cell positional effects are ignorable, resulted in increased dendritogenesis without altering L4 fate specification.
evidence: Supported by in vitro culture experiment data.

claim: Pcdh20- and Dcx double-knockdown neurons tend to exhibit pyramidal morphology even if they are in L4, especially those located near the margin of L4.
source: In vivo, Pcdh20- and Dcx double-knockdown neurons tended to exhibit pyramidal morphology even if they were in L4, especially those located near the margin of L4, also suggesting the primary effect, to some extent at least, of Pcdh20 on cell morphology.
evidence: Supported by double knockdown experiment observations.

claim: Regulation of dendritic morphogenesis by another protocadherin was reported previously.
source: Regulation of dendritic morphogenesis by another protocadherin was also reported previously (Shima et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Loss of Pcdh20 first affects dendrite morphology leading to extensive dendritic arborization when control cells start to exhibit simplification of their complex apical primitive dendrites.
source: Second, in the time-course experiment of Pcdh20 knockdown, we noticed that loss of Pcdh20 first affected the dendrite morphology leading to extensive dendritic arborization, when the control cells already started to exhibit simplification of their complex apical primitive dendrites (Figure 2J,K).
evidence: Supported by time-course experiment observations shown in Figure 2J,K.

claim: Active RhoA rescues the malpositioning caused by Pcdh20 knockdown with reduced arborization of the apical dendrites.
source: Finally, active RhoA rescued the malpositioning caused by Pcdh20 knockdown with reduced arborization of the apical dendrites of the Pcdh20-knockdown neurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by CA-RhoA rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The abnormal dendrites might have caused the Pcdh20-knockdown neurons to become 'stuck' to the MZ.
source: Because the arborized dendrites were predominantly found in the MZ, it is possible that the abnormal dendrites might have caused the knockdown neurons to become 'stuck' to the MZ.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on dendrite localization.

claim: Several members of the protocadherin family exhibit homophilic binding activity.
source: Considering that several members of the protocadherin family exhibit homophilic binding activity (Kim et al., 2007; Morishita and Yagi, 2007; Suzuki, 2000; Takeichi, 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Homophilic interactions may regulate laminar formation through gathering neurons that share the adhesion activity.
source: it is conceivable that homophilic interactions may regulate laminar formation through gathering neurons that share the adhesion activity.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on known protocadherin properties.

claim: The interactions through protocadherins, including Pcdh20, are usually very weak or undetectable.
source: However, since the interactions through protocadherins, including Pcdh20, are usually very weak or undetectable (K.O. and K.N. unpublished data), there may be other ligands that activate Pcdh20 to regulate neuronal positioning.
evidence: Supported by unpublished data from the authors.

claim: There may be other ligands that activate Pcdh20 to regulate neuronal positioning.
source: However, since the interactions through protocadherins, including Pcdh20, are usually very weak or undetectable (K.O. and K.N. unpublished data), there may be other ligands that activate Pcdh20 to regulate neuronal positioning.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on weak protocadherin interactions.

claim: The acquisition of L4-specific characteristics by future L4 neurons coincides with the arrival of TCAs into the lower part of the CP.
source: Since the acquisition of the L4-specific characteristics (e.g., simplification of apical dendrites) by the "future L4 neurons" coincided with the arrival of the TCAs into the lower part of the CP (Lopez-Bendito and Molnar, 2003), we hypothesized that these axons could positively regulate the L4 identity specification.
evidence: Inferred from temporal correlation, with citation.

claim: TCAs are involved in correct subtype specification of L4 neurons.
source: We demonstrated here that TCAs might be involved in correct subtype specification of L4 neurons by the analysis of TCA-deficient Pcdh10 (OL-pc) knockout mice.
evidence: Supported by analysis of Pcdh10 (OL-pc) knockout mice.

claim: Defects in TCAs misspecify L4 identity.
source: The results of other studies also suggested that defects in TCAs misspecify L4 identity (Zhou et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: TCAs instruct the development of modality-specific properties of cortical neurons.
source: and that TCAs instruct the development of modality-specific properties of cortical neurons (Pouchelon et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: TCA absence results in loss of L4 identity and acquisition of some L2/3 characteristics.
source: Here, we showed that TCA absence resulted in loss of L4 identity and, surprisingly, instead acquisition of some L2/3 characteristics, which recapitulated the phenotypes observed in Pcdh20 or Dcx knockdown
evidence: Supported by analysis of Pcdh10 (OL-pc) knockout mice.

claim: Defects in synaptic activity from TCAs to cortical neurons do not appear to be involved in subtype specification of L4 neurons in mice.
source: It was reported that defects in synaptic activity from TCAs to cortical neurons did not appear to be involved in subtype specification of L4 neurons in mice (Hannan et al., 2001; Iwasato et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Complete blockade of thalamocortical neurotransmission results in perturbed development of L4 neurons, but initial specification appears largely normal.
source: A more recent study showed that complete blockade of thalamocortical neurotransmission resulted in perturbed development of L4 neurons. Initial specification of cortical neurons, however, appeared largely normal (Li et al., 2013), which occurs through the first week after birth, at the stage when specification failure was already observed in our mouse model.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: A transmembrane protein is involved in subtype specification in the post-migratory stage.
source: Finally, another intriguing finding of this study was the apparent involvement of a transmembrane protein in the subtype specification in the post-migratory stage.
evidence: Inferred from Pcdh20 being a transmembrane protein with post-migratory function.

claim: The environment around immature neurons could influence the subtype specification of neurons.
source: This suggested that the environment around the immature neurons could also influence the subtype specification of the neurons.
evidence: Inferred from transmembrane protein involvement suggesting environmental influence.

claim: It is not known whether subtype-specific transcription factors are induced intrinsically or in response to the extracellular environment.
source: Although postmitotic expressions of fate determinants, such as subtype-specific transcription factors, have been observed in the immature CP, it is not known whether these factors are induced intrinsically downstream of the fate determinants in the progenitor cells or in response to the extracellular environment.
evidence: Statement of current knowledge gap.
